summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743 passed the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention on 9 May 2012, was promulgated on 24 May 2012, and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. Emergency decree DNU 62/2025, published in February 2025, modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for people under 18, which Reuters reported as a ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Decree DNU 61/2025 of the same month re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere; it bars people who have legally changed their gender from being held in women's prisons when detained for sexual offences or violence against women.

National protection machinery has been dismantled. The national administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the twelve-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

Violence reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity across the year, a ten-year record averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026 puts 32% of those crimes inside police stations and penal facilities, records security-force violence rising from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and shows trans women and travestis concentrating 62.5% of victims, 142 cases, with most perpetrators drawn from security personnel and unknown assailants.

The operative risk on the ground is police identification and detention. On 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women, writing several of them up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one. Activists described the operation as a new episode of illegal persecution.

Judicial protection against gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible LGBTQ scene and tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law alongside the national femicide registry, making it where a state response is most likely to be present. FALGBT and legal experts called both February 2025 decrees illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina retains the strongest statutory position in Latin America on gender recognition, and the country's record on marriage equality and anti-discrimination legislation predates the current executive posture. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, nonetheless records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-sexuality organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the national government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Agencia Presentes described the 2025 hate-crime figure as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Legal scholars and advocacy bodies contest the constitutional footing of the February 2025 decrees, arguing that emergency decree powers cannot be used to rewrite a statute passed by parliament, and have signalled litigation. The Supreme Court's April 2025 handling of the Sacayán case shows the limits of that contest: the sentence stands, but the aggravating basis for treating the killing as gender-motivated was not restored.
localsOnly:
Residents who changed legal gender under Law 26.743 keep that recognition without surgery or judicial sign-off, but the February 2025 decrees alter the position for minors, who can no longer receive gender-affirming surgery or hormone therapy, and for trans people held in the penal system. DNU 61/2025 was drafted to be adopted by sub-national governments, so its application inside the city depends on local adherence.

Public-sector employment protections have been eroded at source: the Trans Labor Quota Law had reserved at least 1% of state jobs for trans workers, and the national administration dismissed trans employees hired under it. The Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry no longer exists, and INADI, which handled discrimination complaints, has been closed.

The city's own anti-discrimination statute has been in force since 1996 and continues to operate alongside national and provincial anti-discrimination laws. Residents also live with the administration of the national femicide registry and the employment quota inside the city, which is where enforcement capacity and record-keeping are most concentrated.

Harm is concentrated in encounters with the security forces: of the 227 recorded 2025 hate crimes, roughly a third occurred in police stations and penal facilities, and trans women and travestis made up 62.5% of victims.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the City of Buenos Aires has formally adhered to DNU 61/2025, and therefore how the decree's prison-housing rules are applied inside the city, is unresolved in the sources consulted.

The outcome of the litigation signalled by FALGBT and legal experts against DNU 61/2025 and DNU 62/2025 is unresolved; no court ruling on either decree is sourced here.

The year of the 18 September police station 18 operation described in the current record is not specified in the source material, and the penalty attached to an article 81 Contravention Code citation for lacking documents is not sourced.

Whether the travesticidio aggravating circumstance will be reinstated in other pending cases after the April 2025 Supreme Court decision is unresolved; the sources address only the Sacayán line of cases.

Outright International's March 2026 assessments are recorded at country level and are not disaggregated to Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires.
